extraction.title: Industry Growth and Political Spending: Research Plan
extraction.document_type: Research plan (Paul's own research note; specifies tests and sources, reports no estimated results)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass: all 301 lines of the 29,981-character file (_text/46495cfa916e.txt), Sections 1-9. No annotation files exist (annot_sha12s is empty), so paul_markup is empty and nothing was dropped. p.note is true, so the author is treated as Paul. No ext/rel override files existed. Metadata hints verified: title, author, 2026 date and research-note venue are correct; the document is a plan, not a results paper.
extraction.research_question: Do industries spend differently on politics (federal campaign contributions and lobbying) when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow? Does a published industry growth forecast predict subsequent spending, and do expectations about House and Senate control help explain spending?
extraction.theory: Better performance could supply more money for political spending; weak performance or a weak forecast could instead prompt spending to seek favorable policy. The sign of the relationship is to be estimated, not assumed.
extraction.data: Target panel of annual sector-year observations, 2008-2025, for nine sectors where comparable data exist: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance, auto manufacturing, crypto, Credit Arms, Fintech, Property and Casualty insurance, Telecom. Odd years retained; incomplete 2026 excluded. Unit is sector-year; spending in millions of 2025 dollars. Sources: IBISWorld revenue and archived forecasts; Mentat/FEC contributions split by job tier; Melange LDA and LobbyView lobbying; IEM congressional control forecasts; Minneapolis Fed CPI. Final N is not yet fixed: verified contribution years overlap the congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022. Strict annual growth inputs: 53 in the original collection, 86 in the expanded nine-sector grid.
extraction.method: Multiple linear regression by OLS with a separate intercept per sector (sector fixed effects). Contributions: Y_it = a_i + b X_it + c Pres_t + d Midterm_t + e ExpectedDemHouse_t + f ExpectedDemSenate_t + error. Lobbying adds CurrentDemHouse_t and CurrentDemSenate_t. X is prior actual growth, same-year actual growth, or predicted growth (tests C1-C3 and L1-L3). Growth in percentage points. Job-tier extension: pooled model with sector-by-tier baselines and growth x tier terms, Employee as reference. Chamber extension: linear model of Democratic share of contributions. Further extensions: prior and predicted growth together; year indicators in place of national controls; logged spending for positive observations. Simple regression only to illustrate scatterplots.
extraction.identification: No causal identification is claimed. Identifying variation is within-sector over time, after election-cycle and congressional-expectation controls. Predicted growth is taken from the latest IBISWorld report published by December 31 of the prior year, so it precedes the spending year. Congressional expectations are concurrent IEM averages and may not be known before all spending in a year. Results are framed as associations consistent with a response to public forecasts, not knowledge of firms' private expectations.
extraction.scope: US federal political spending by nine industry sectors, 2008-2025: candidate-committee contributions (personal versus organizational/PAC channels) and lobbying expenditures. Sector membership follows workbook rosters (40 company names) and industry proxies: Credit Arms is a proxy for workbook companies, Telecom is analyzed at component level, and Fintech lacks a comparable annual series. Life insurance and auto manufacturing are not among the published workbooks checked.

key_findings.finding: Design is OLS with sector fixed effects and six core tests: C1-C3 explain contributions and L1-L3 explain lobbying, each with prior actual, same-year actual, or predicted growth as the growth regressor.
key_findings.numbers: 6 core tests; growth in percentage points; spending in millions of 2025 dollars

key_findings.finding: Predicted growth must come from the latest IBISWorld report published by December 31 of year t-1 that forecasts year t, using numerator and denominator from the same vintage.
key_findings.location: Section 4, Predicting growth: preserve the original forecast date
key_findings.numbers: Example: report estimates 2019 revenue at 100 and 2020 at 105, giving 5 percent

key_findings.finding: Readiness check: verified contribution years overlap the prepared congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022, too little annual variation to identify the full control specification.
IBISWorld collection size: 63 original reports yielding 53 strict annual sector-year values; the expanded nine-sector grid has 86 strict annual revenue-growth inputs with explicit missing rows.
key_findings.numbers: 63 reports; 53 then 86 strict annual inputs; 12 supplemental observations kept separate

key_findings.finding: Banking and credit-union revenue include 2006, while life insurance and auto extracts start in 2007, leaving their 2008 lagged-growth observation incomplete.
key_findings.numbers: 2006 start for banks and credit unions; 2007 for life and auto

key_findings.finding: Crypto has only one verified original forecast: a Statista U.S. cryptocurrency-platform revenue forecast for 2025 of minus 3.78 percent, available by December 26, 2024, kept as a separate proxy.
Telecom is kept at component level (wireless and cable archives, 36 reports) because cable's revenue definition changes; Fintech has only dated multi-year projections and no comparable annual series.
key_findings.location: Section 6A, table rows for Telecom and Fintech

key_findings.finding: Congressional control forecasts (IEM) are available 2008-2022 only; 2023-2025 are missing, and the later election result must never substitute for a missing forecast.

Job-tier test uses a pooled model with sector-by-tier baselines and growth-by-tier interactions, Employee as reference; the existing Employee class includes unrecognized-title fallbacks that must be flagged.
key_findings.numbers: Chief slope term q; Middle Management slope term r

key_findings.finding: Partisan direction is tested with a per-chamber Democratic share outcome, D/(D+R), with zero denominators set to missing; party, presidential and other committee flows are not assigned to a chamber without a defensible mapping.

Lobbying outcome must keep expenses_total and income_total distinct, since client reports and outside-registrant receipts can refer to overlapping money; the four-sector LDA aggregate does not cover all nine sectors.
key_findings.numbers: 2 recorded measures analyzed separately; LDA annual rows 2021-2025 plus partial 2026

key_findings.finding: Inference caution: with few independent sector groups, ordinary independent-row OLS standard errors are not sufficient for strong significance claims, so repeated observations and small-sample uncertainty must be assessed.

extraction.measures: Dependent variables: annual federal candidate contributions (personal and organizational/PAC channels) and lobbying expenditures, in millions of inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars using annual CPI multiplier 321.9 over CPI. Independent variables: actual growth as 100 times (revenue ratio minus 1); prior-year growth; predicted growth from the report vintage; expected Democratic House and Senate control on a 0-1 scale (IEM, converted from Republican probability); current Democratic House and Senate control (1/0); presidential and midterm indicators. Job tiers: Chief, Middle Management, Employee. Partisan outcome: Democratic share of contributions per chamber.
limitations: Plan only: no estimated results are reported in the document.
Few independent sector groups (nine planned, fewer usable); ordinary OLS standard errors understate uncertainty; repeated observations must be accounted for.
Verified contribution years overlap congressional forecasts only in 2021-2022, so the full control specification is not yet identified.
IEM congressional forecasts are concurrent averages, not necessarily known before all spending in the year, and are missing for 2023-2025.
IBISWorld forecasts proxy public expectations only; they do not reveal private firm forecasts or whether a donor read the report.
Credit Arms is an industry proxy for workbook companies with OneMain and equipment-finance scope differences needing sensitivity checks.
Telecom is component-level; Fintech lacks a comparable annual series; crypto has one verified forecast.
Auto 2011-2012 uses a car and light-truck component reconstruction and needs a check excluding it; several forecast price bases differ and some values are inferred.
Chief classification uses a non-date-specific executive-name override; historical tier comparisons need role at donation date or a sensitivity test.
Employee tier includes unrecognized-title fallbacks; lobbying has no donor job-tier split in verified sources.
Lobbying: expenses_total and income_total measure overlapping money and cannot be simply added; older undifferentiated amount totals are not comparable without checking.
Historical contribution coverage before 2021 is not established in the local workbook extracts; FEC bulk data may be needed.
Sources cover only the selected sectors and are not an exhaustive archive of forecasts.

summary_md: Paul's own research plan (dated 2026-09-25) for testing whether industries spend more or less on federal politics when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow. It specifies OLS with a separate intercept per sector, six core tests (C1-C3 contributions, L1-L3 lobbying, each with prior actual, same-year actual, or IBISWorld predicted growth), election-cycle dummies and IEM expected-control covariates, plus job-tier and per-chamber Democratic-share extensions. Its strongest contributions are discipline rules: predicted growth must come from a report vintage published before the spending year, missing forecasts stay missing, null results are kept, and independent-row OLS errors are ruled insufficient with nine or fewer sector clusters. It reports no estimates, and its own readiness check says contributions overlap the IEM forecasts only in 2021-2022. The document is the north star of the built sector growth study (Mentat sector_growth_study, in R). The build honours the inference caution with a wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector and Holm adjustment, but departs from the plan in three places: log outcomes rather than dollar levels, a retrospective 2023-2026 expected-control series plus 538 robustness filling the IEM gap, and added Tossup and trend terms. Results recorded in the brain (UNVERIFIED, single path): L3 on LobbyView lobbying b 0.242 million 2025 USD per pp (p 0.033, Holm 0.1125) flips to -0.477 under year FE, growth adds no adjusted R2, and the annual partisan SHIFT is -0.04 (p 0.76). So far the plan's question is answered as no stable growth signal, which bears directly on the live giving forecast that still feeds IBISWorld growth into general giving at 50/50.

bearings.paper_claim: Six core tests C1-C3 (contributions) and L1-L3 (lobbying), each with prior actual, same-year actual or predicted growth as the regressor; Y in millions of 2025 USD; X in percentage points; keep all six results including nulls; nine planned sectors give few independent groups so ordinary independent-row OLS errors are not sufficient for strong significance claims.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2 (six core tests table), Section 3 (equations and units), Section 5 (final paragraph)
bearings.system_side: R build runs C1-C3 on contributions_real_m and L1-L3 on lobbying DVs with the growth regressors in SGS_GROWTH; controls are pres_year, midterm_year, exp_dem_house, exp_dem_senate, plus cur_dem_house and cur_dem_senate for lobbying; sector baselines; inference is wild cluster restricted bootstrap-t by sector with Webb six-point weights, enumerated when 6^G is at most 9999; Holm adjustment across pre-specified families. Main outcomes are levels in millions; log DVs appear only as robustness variants R-log and R-logFE on L-LV. No Tossup or trend regressor is in either control set.

Rel summary says the build models log giving with Tossup and trend terms. Code: main DVs are levels in millions; log is only the R-log and R-logFE robustness family; no Tossup or trend regressor is in the growth control sets. Remove or rewrite this departure.

Rel flags a possible conflict between the 2023-2026 retrospective expectation series and the plan's timing rule. Code (sgs_config.R:185) records it as Paul's explicit ruling, labelled RETROSPECTIVE / NOWCAST, with STRICT variants. State it that way.

meta.title: Review: industry growth and political spending

extraction.title: Review: industry growth and political spending
extraction.document_type: Internal research-design review note (self-described as not an empirical result; no models estimated)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (30,563 chars, 221 lines): front matter, overall verdict, risk ranking, starting formula, sections 1-14, data and citation corrections table, literature list, design steps. No _annots files exist (annot_sha12s empty), so paul_markup is empty. Author taken from metadata per note:true instruction; the text itself names no author and reviews a brief titled Astra_Review_Brief_Sector_Growth_and_Political_Spending.md. Cited URLs were not fetched; claims are taken as stated in the text. Metadata title and venue judged correct. key_findings capped at 12 of 13 candidates; dropped the Section 12 policy-salience finding (hearing-count control; catalog listed through 2021, which is in limitations).
extraction.research_question: Does prior-year real industry growth predict subsequent organizational political spending (corporate and trade-association PAC contributions to congressional candidates, and reported LDA lobbying expenditure), and do election expectations (probability of chamber control) predict where PAC giving goes across parties, incumbents and committee members? The growth association is the main question; expectations are a separate, exploratory question.
extraction.theory: Three mechanisms, not a predetermined sign: favorable performance can expand capacity; poor performance can raise demand for relief while reducing resources; threatened policy losses can induce spending in either economic state. Majority status has value (Cox and Magar). Committee access drives reallocation (Powell and Grimmer). Regulatory shocks can lower output and raise lobbying at once, producing a negative association without distress-driven behavior.
extraction.data: Not yet assembled; no N estimated. Unit: industry-year. Case analysis uses five sectors; broad panel may use five to ten sectors or all insurance carriers. Proposed common panel 2008-2024 (about 18 annual observations; 2025 only after source audit). Outcomes: FEC committee-to-candidate PAC disbursements (DIME v4.0 covers 1979-2024 public itemized files, excluding CRP/NIMSP-sourced records); LDA LD-2 lobbying, quarterly from 2008. Growth: BEA real value added. Expectations: chamber-control markets (Iowa Electronic Markets, incomplete odd-year coverage) or archived forecasts, about nine elections, six realized chamber flips. Salience: Policy Agendas hearings catalog (listed through 2021) and Unified Agenda editions.
extraction.method: Main model: log S_it = alpha_i + lambda_t + beta g_{i,t-1} + e, with sector and year effects, estimated separately for PAC contributions and lobbying (never summed). Growth g = 100 (V_t / V_{t-1} - 1) on raw real value added. Alternatives: PPML exponential conditional mean if genuine zeros exist; log initial sector size at t-2 as a control; split growth into g+ = max(g,0) and g- = max(-g,0) for asymmetry; dynamic FE only as sensitivity (Bruno bias correction; Arellano-Bond or system GMM not recommended with five to ten sectors). Expectations study: RShare = sector/chamber baseline + coefficient times earlier P + coefficient times current control + limited calendar controls, with a fractional-response sensitivity. Inference: small-sample cluster corrections, restricted wild-cluster bootstrap, cluster leverage, leave-one-sector-out, Driscoll-Kraay only as sensitivity, randomization inference only with a defensible assignment argument.
extraction.identification: Identification rests on within-sector variation in lagged real growth net of sector means and common year shocks. Lagging fixes ordering but does not establish causality; the Bruno correction does not solve endogeneity in current-year growth. Expectations identification comes from election-cycle variation in earlier control probabilities, with roughly nine elections and six realized flips, so the review treats those estimates as exploratory. Chamber-by-year effects absorb chamber-specific probabilities in a pooled panel.
extraction.measures: Spending: inflation-adjusted PAC contributions and lobbying expenditure (logs). Growth: raw percent change in BEA real value added; standardized growth only as secondary presentation. P: earlier probability of Republican chamber control. M: current Republican control. RShare: Republican share of candidate giving (undefined when total partisan giving is zero). Secondary: incumbent share, committee-member share, expected seat change, lagged count of relevant congressional hearings, pending regulatory proceedings (sensitivity).
extraction.scope: Prospective design for US federal politics: corporate and trade-association PAC disbursements to congressional candidates, LDA lobbying, BEA-classified industries, 2008-2024 (2025 if audited). Excludes unregistered advocacy, state politics, and industry-affiliated individual giving, party contributions, super PAC financing and independent expenditures, which are to be analyzed as separate channels.

key_findings.finding: Make prior real industry growth the main analysis; treat election expectations and partisan allocation as a separate, more exploratory analysis because more industries add information about growth but not more national elections.
key_findings.numbers: No estimates; 14 numbered sections of recommendations

key_findings.finding: The measures (asset growth, profits, premiums, production, crypto valuations) do not yet share a common economic mechanism; z-scores change scale, not meaning.
Repeating a national forecast across industries adds no independent forecast shocks; coverage, timing, common shocks and roughly nine elections matter more than total row count.
Shift plus current control is a reparameterization of probability plus current control; the current-control coefficient holding P fixed is g minus f.

key_findings.finding: A contraction indicator is not an asymmetric slope; define contraction on raw real growth below zero and use g+ and g- with separate coefficients to test asymmetry.

summary_md: A design review dated 2026-09-24, filed as Paul's research note, of the Astra brief that became the Mentat sector growth study. It estimates nothing. Its core advice: make prior-year real growth the main question and fit log spending on sector and year fixed effects plus lagged raw percent growth (g(t-1)), separately for organizational PAC giving and LDA lobbying, never summed. Treat election expectations as a separate, exploratory study, because more sectors do not create more elections (about 9 elections, 6 chamber flips). It also says three of the brief's specifications do not test their hypotheses: a contraction dummy is not an asymmetric slope (use g+ and g-); Shift = P - M plus current control only reparameterizes P plus M; and a unified-government term cannot separate expected from current control. On data, it says not to fill missing control probabilities with realized results. It says 538 models that use fundraising create a feedback loop, so a polls-only sensitivity is better. It warns that LDA in-house totals already include retained-firm payments and association dues. With five sectors, it says, use the restricted wild-cluster bootstrap and leave-one-sector-out checks. Against the system as built, several points were adopted: raw percent growth, g_pos/g_neg splits, the restricted wild-cluster bootstrap with a few-cluster guard, LOSO/LOYO, the 538 Lite seat forecasts, and lobbying series that are never summed. Others were not. The primary models use dollar levels with national phase and expected-control controls, and year fixed effects and logs are only robustness checks. The giving outcome is Mentat general giving across all recipient types. The 2023/2025 expected control was filled after the fact by Paul's ruling. The later Codex audit vindicated the review's main warning: the L3-LV lobbying slope of +0.352 flipped to -0.477 under sector and year fixed effects (UNSTRATIFIED, 5 sectors, 2008-2023).

extraction.method: Four actual-growth OLS-style regressions (k=1 previous-year growth; k=0 same-year growth; each for contributions and lobbying): Spending(sector, year) = sector baseline + b x Growth(sector, year-k) + c x PresidentialYear + d x MidtermYear + e x ExpectedDemHouse + f x ExpectedDemSenate + error. Plus two predicted-growth tests using the prior-year forecast for year t in place of actual growth; six core tests total per the linked plan. Party direction: Democratic share = Dem / (Dem + Rep), separately for House and Senate recipients; missing when denominator is zero. Job-level comparison: sector x year x tier (Chief, Middle Management, Employee) for contributions only. No regressions have been run yet.

summary_md: Paul's September 25, 2026 source check is the data inventory and design note behind the Mentat sector growth study. At that point no regressions had been run. It lists IBISWorld real-revenue growth for four sectors: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance and auto. It also has a 72-row sector-year panel for 2008-2025, election-year dummies and actual chamber control checked against the House and Senate histories. Expected control (conditional IEM measures) covers 2008-2022 only, and CPI multipliers convert spending to 2025 dollars. The note specifies six core regressions: spending on sector baseline plus growth (same-year, previous-year or predicted), presidential and midterm dummies, and expected Democratic House and Senate control, each run for contributions and lobbying. It also defines a Democratic share by chamber and a Chief / Middle Management / Employee tier split. The built system implements this design almost exactly: sgs_registry.R carries the same three growth variables and the same four controls. The IBISWorld lagged real-growth path also feeds the live giving forecast's 50/50 budget term. The note is now stale. The study has since moved to nine sectors and a 2020-2026 window, and its results are mostly null. Growth adds no adjusted R2 (0.884717 vs 0.884690, LobbyView lobbying). The predicted-growth lobbying coefficient flips from +0.352 to -0.477 under sector and year fixed effects, and its Holm p rises from 0.0375 to 0.1125. The partisan-shift test gives -0.04 (p 0.76, 2021-25). These are agent runs, partly reproduced by a Codex review, so they stay UNVERIFIED under DE-062. The note's warnings still hold: keep blanks as missing, do not deflate IBISWorld twice, and treat expected-control means as concurrent, not causal.

The lobbying specification adds cur_dem_house and cur_dem_senate (SGS_L_CONTROLS, line 34), which the note treats as optional rather than core.

The LobbyView tests use the 2008-2025 fallback. The claim that same-year growth is outside a real forecast's information set is not in the note and could not be verified, so it is removed.

summary_issues: Window misstated: the summary says the built study runs a 2020-2026 window. sgs_registry.R and sgs_config.R set the primary window to 2020-2025 (R8), with a fallback inside 2008-2025.
Sector count not established: the summary says nine sectors. sgs_registry.R lines 242 and 463 describe seven study sectors plus community_banks. Treat nine as unverified.

Misattributed quote in paul_alignment: the phrase seems to confirm does not appear in the note. The trend-over-significance rule is not stated in the note either. The note contains no regression results to comment on.

Unlocated figures: MAE 3.63 vs 3.99, growth beating naive in 45 percent of targets, 264 tests with 72 estimable, and retrospective 2023 expected-control fill were not found in the sector_growth_study folder by grep. Unverified.

Numbers present in the study's own review file: sgs_review.R lines 33-35 hold L3-LV base 0.352 and yearfe -0.477, with Holm p moving 0.0375 to 0.1125; lines 237-238 hold adjusted R2 0.884717 vs 0.884690. This is the study's own Codex review, not an independent second path, so it stays UNVERIFIED under DE-062.

Partisan-shift result -0.04 (p 0.76, 2021-25) only partly confirmed: coefficients near -0.0428 and -0.0405 appear in build_receipt_08_contributions_by_chamber.json, but the p-value and window were not located.
Design fidelity overstated: the lobbying tests add cur_dem_house and cur_dem_senate (sgs_registry.R line 34), which the note treats as optional, so the built design is not exactly the note's design.

Giving-forecast link: the 50/50 budget term fed by the IBISWorld lagged real-growth path is supported by code comments (giving_forecast.py lines 1393-1398). The no-out-of-sample-support point rests on the backtest figures, which could not be located.
gaps_exposed: The note is stale against the system. It says no regressions have run, uses a 2008-2025 four-sector panel and leaves 2023-2025 expected control absent. The study now covers nine sectors and the 2020-2026 cycles, has run 264 tests (72 estimable) and filled 2023 expected control retrospectively.

Expected control for 2023 (Nov-2024 calls) and 2025 (Sep-2026 snapshot) is measured after the year. A strict forecast needs available_at gates, which the note's annual-mean convention does not provide.

Contribution outcomes before 2021 (2020 now collected) do not exist locally. The note's 18-year contribution panel therefore cannot be built, and the core contribution tests C1-C3 rest on a few cycles.
Life insurance and auto lobbying series are not cached, and crypto has no IBISWorld growth series, so two or three original sectors stay thin.
There are few clusters (4-9 sectors) for the wild sector-cluster bootstrap. With 2 sectors the bootstrap cannot reach p below 0.056 (sgs_registry.R:22).
The live cycle model's IBISWorld 50/50 growth term has no out-of-sample support from the study's own backtest (growth beat naive in 45% of targets).
flags: The header (nine-sector expansion: 72 reports, 86 growth inputs, a 162-row scaffold) and the four-sector body are unreconciled within the note.

Pooled growth coefficient: the note's single b across sectors with a sector baseline must be quoted with per-sector strata or an UNSTRATIFIED label. The built code attaches strata and a stratification label (sgs_estimate.R:377, 401).
ExpectedDemHouse/Senate are year-level. Year fixed effects can test growth but cannot identify them, and the predicted-growth lobbying sign flipped (+0.352 to -0.477) once year FE were added.
The Employee tier includes unrecognized-title fallbacks, so it is not verified rank-and-file. Any tier comparison must say so.
The study results quoted here are agent analyses, partly reproduced by the Codex review. They stay UNVERIFIED under DE-062 until a second path reproduces each one.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-025 or D-104..D-108; the note makes no network or reciprocity claims.
paul_alignment: There are no bibliography entries; this is Paul's own note. The built study follows its design closely, so the two agree on method. The note is stale: the regressions have since run on nine sectors over 2020-2026. The evidence does not support a growth-to-spending link: growth adds no adjusted R2, the lobbying lead flips under year FE, there is no partisan shift (-0.04, p 0.76) and naive forecasting wins the backtest. Paul's 'seems to confirm' for lobbying is premature, and even under his trend-over-significance rule the sign is not stable.

related.why: LobbyView is a firm-level LDA database. The note does not name LobbyView as its source for the bank and CU aggregates, so this is background for the LDA measure, not confirmed same-data.
Paul's unpublished client report on financial-services political money covers bank and credit-union sections, overlapping the note's sectors. The note does not cite it.

Its title reports low overlap between lobbying and PAC spending, which is consistent with running contributions and lobbying as separate outcomes. The note does not state this reasoning; it is the analyst's inference.
Its title covers strategic and sequential links between donations and lobbying, a lead-lag framing the note does not use.
Its title covers corporate lobbying, PAC spending and market concentration, a related economic-driver design.
Its title and tags cover the cryptocurrency lobby and PAC spending, the sector the note handles only through a proxy.
